scales.name: Minor Pentatonic
scales.description: The foundation — 5 essential notes that always work over minor keys.

progressions.description: The all-minor i-iv-v. No leading tone, no 2, no 6 — every chord root sits on one of the five pentatonic notes, which is why this progression feels inseparable from the scale.
The descending minor rock cadence (Stairway / Dio territory). The roots 1, b7, b6 trace pentatonic-friendly motion, and the b6 chord hints at Aeolian color while staying pentatonic-safe for soloing.

scales.name: Major Pentatonic
scales.description: The major counterpart — bright, uplifting, great for country and pop.

progressions.description: Primary-color tonality. Major pentatonic deliberately omits the 4 and 7 — the exact notes that would clash over I, IV, V — so every pentatonic lick lands safely across all three chords.
The 50s doo-wop progression. vi is the relative minor of I and shares four of its five pentatonic notes, so the scale stays musical through the minor detour.

scales.name: Natural Minor (Aeolian)
scales.description: Full minor scale — pentatonic + 2 and b6. Darker, more complete minor sound.

progressions.description: The Andalusian / pop-minor cycle. Moves through all three major chords available in Aeolian (bIII, bVI, bVII), emphasizing the b6 and b7 that distinguish natural minor from pentatonic.
All-minor i-iv-v. The v is minor (not V7) because natural minor has no raised 7th — this is the un-resolved, soft cadence that makes Aeolian sound modal rather than classical.

scales.name: Dorian
scales.description: Minor pentatonic + 2 and 6. THE jam mode — Santana, Allman Bros, funk, and the signature sound of lofi jazz vamps.

progressions.description: THE Dorian vamp. The major IV is Dorian's calling card — the natural 6 (which is the major 3rd of IV) is the single note that separates Dorian from Aeolian, so this progression puts the defining pitch right in your face.

Both chords are diatonic to Dorian, and crucially ii is minor (not half-diminished as in Aeolian). A tight funk/Santana oscillation where the natural 6 and natural 2 of the mode both show up as chord tones.
Extended version of the Dorian vamp. The 9 on i highlights the natural 2, and the 13 on IV highlights the natural 6 — the two notes Dorian adds on top of minor pentatonic.
Three fully-diatonic Dorian chords in a row. IV7 and bVIImaj7 both contain the natural 6, and bVIImaj7's major 7 is the b7 of the key — a walk-down that lives entirely inside the mode.

scales.name: Mixolydian
scales.description: Major scale with b7. Blues-rock staple, dominant chord territory.

progressions.description: The classic Mixolydian cadence (Sweet Home Alabama, Sympathy for the Devil). bVII is the mode's defining chord — it contains the b7 that turns a major scale into Mixolydian.
Double-dominant blues-rock vamp. I7 literally spells out 1-3-5-b7 of Mixolydian, and IV7's b7 is the 3rd of the key — the scale and the chords share DNA.
Funky extensions on the same vamp. I13 stacks 1-3-5-b7-9-13, which is six of the seven Mixolydian notes — you're essentially playing the scale as a chord.
Modal walk through the three major-quality chords of Mixolydian. The mode has a unique major IV (unlike Dorian) AND a major bVII (unlike Ionian), and this progression features both.

scales.name: Harmonic Minor
scales.description: Aeolian + raised 7th. The dramatic interval between b6 and 7 creates tension.

progressions.description: The reason harmonic minor exists. Natural minor's v is minor and doesn't resolve strongly; raising the 7th turns v into a proper dominant V7, creating the half-step leading-tone pull back to i.
Classical minor cadence. The augmented 2nd between b6 (in iv) and 7 (in V7) is harmonic minor's signature exotic interval — you can hear it in the voice leading from Fm to G7 in A minor.

scales.name: Phrygian
scales.description: The darkest common mode — b2 gives that Spanish/metal flavor.

progressions.description: The signature Phrygian move. The b2 is the mode's defining note — one half-step above the root — and bII is literally a chord built on that note. Two chords, total mode identity.
Flamenco oscillation. Sits entirely in the lower half of the scale (1, b2, b3) so the b2 half-step tension keeps re-asserting itself instead of dissolving into brighter territory.

scales.name: Lydian
scales.description: Major with #4. Dreamy, otherworldly — perfect for ambient and ethereal textures.

progressions.description: The signature Lydian sound. A major II chord only exists in Lydian — its major 3rd IS the #4 of the key, the exact note that makes this mode Lydian instead of Ionian.
Imaj7 establishes the dreamy, resolved home base; II provides the floating tension without ever fully leaving Lydian. Both chords are fully diatonic and together spell out 6 of the 7 mode notes.
Note II is II7 (not IImaj7) — in Lydian, II's 7th is the b7-of-the-II-chord which equals the root of the key. iii7 is a diatonic minor-7 landing, and the whole loop lives entirely inside Lydian.

scales.name: Melodic Minor
scales.description: Jazz workhorse — minor with raised 6th and 7th. Smooth and sophisticated.

progressions.description: Jazz ii-V-i in melodic minor. The m(maj7) tonic is the scale's signature chord (using the raised 7), and V7alt can be voiced directly from the same melodic minor scale a half-step up — one scale covers everything.

IV is dominant (not minor or major 7) because melodic minor's raised 6 becomes the major-3rd of IV while the b7 of the key is still IV's b7. Bright, unresolved, and impossible to get from Aeolian or Dorian.

Jazzy minor turnaround. vim7b5 is genuinely diatonic to melodic minor (A-C-Eb-G in C melodic minor) — unlike natural minor where vi would be major — so this progression showcases melodic minor's unique chord colors.

scales.name: Phrygian Dominant
scales.description: 5th mode of harmonic minor. Extremely dramatic — Middle Eastern flavor.

progressions.description: Spanish/Middle-Eastern cadence. The major I (with natural 3) paired with bII a half-step above captures the whole mode in two chords — it's why this sounds instantly like flamenco or klezmer.

The classic flamenco cycle. The major I sits against the minor iv (the mode's b6 in action) and the bII resolves chromatically down to I — the three characteristic moves of Phrygian dominant in one loop.

scales.name: Whole Tone
scales.description: All whole steps — no resolution, pure floating ambiguity.

progressions.description: Every triad in whole-tone is augmented (because every interval is a whole step). This vamp captures the mode's symmetric, leaning-forward quality — no chord wants to resolve anywhere.

Whole tone's most common real-world use. A 7#5 chord is literally 4 notes of the whole-tone scale (1-3-#5-b7), so this is the scale Debussy and jazz players reach for when they see an altered dominant.

scales.name: Diminished (H-W)
scales.description: Alternating half and whole steps. Maximum tension — perfect for horror.

progressions.description: Diminished is a symmetrical scale — any dim7 chord repeats every minor 3rd. Idim7 and bIIIdim7 are enharmonically the same four notes, which is why diminished grooves feel suspended and cyclical.
The H-W diminished scale contains a full dominant 7b9 chord (1-3-5-b7-b9) on its root. This is the go-to scale for soloing over altered V7b9 chords in jazz.

scales.name: Major (Ionian)
scales.description: The standard major scale — happy, resolved, the foundation of Western music.

progressions.description: The 50s/pop standard. Every chord is diatonic, the roots spell a classic circle-of-fifths-adjacent motion, and the vi adds a touch of relative minor without ever leaving Ionian.

The most important progression in Western music. Every note is diatonic to major — the V7 contains the leading-tone 7 that resolves to the root of I, which is the central harmonic move of tonal music.
The jazz 'I-vi-ii-V' turnaround with extended 7th chords. All four chords are diatonic to major — together they contain every note of the scale, making this a perfect loop to practice Ionian over.

The extended turnaround starting from iii — a jazz walk-down through all the diatonic minor-7 chords of major. Common in rhythm changes bridges; solos over this have 7 whole scale notes to work with at all times.

scales.name: Locrian
scales.description: The most unstable mode — b5 removes any sense of resolution. Rare but powerful for tension.

progressions.description: Locrian's tonic is half-diminished (b5 is the defining note). bVmaj7 is a tritone away from i and captures the mode's unsettled center — there's no stable point of rest, which IS the Locrian sound.
The only way Locrian 'resolves' is to step away from it. The bII (major) creates a half-step pull that wants to escape the instability of Im7b5 — a rare but effective modal gesture.

scales.name: Blues Scale
scales.description: Minor pentatonic + the blue note (b5). Essential for blues and rock.

progressions.description: The foundational blues progression. All three chords are dominant 7s — which means they all contain a b7 that matches the scale's b7, and the blue note (b5) passes through all of them as a chromatic tension.
Minor blues vamp. The scale's ambiguous b3/3 relationship lets a minor i sit next to a dominant IV without sounding wrong — the b5 'blue note' is the glue that makes both chord qualities feel bluesy.

scales.name: Bebop Dominant
scales.description: Mixolydian + a chromatic passing tone (major 7). Lands chord tones on downbeats — the go-to for walking bebop lines over lofi jazz dominants.

progressions.description: A Mixolydian dominant-7 vamp. Bebop dominant is Mixolydian with an added passing-tone major 7 — all the same chords work, but the extra note gives you an 8-note scale that lands chord tones on every downbeat.

This scale was literally designed for the V7 of a ii-V-I. Starting on V's root, the eighth notes alternate chord tone / non-chord tone — which is why bebop lines sound so effortlessly 'inside' over the V.
Rhythm-changes turnaround. Use bebop dominant over both VI7 and V7 — the scale works for any dominant chord, and running it through two of them back-to-back is textbook bebop vocabulary.

scales.name: Lydian Dominant
scales.description: 4th mode of melodic minor — a major scale with #4 and b7. The floaty, slightly unresolved sound under lofi jazz dominant 7#11 chords.

progressions.description: I7#11 IS Lydian Dominant as a chord: 1-3-5-b7-#11 is five of the seven scale notes stacked vertically. bVIImaj7 is diatonic to the mode and lets the sound breathe without resolving.
II is dominant-7 in Lydian Dominant (not major-7): its major 3rd is the key's #4. Both chords are dominant quality, both contain the b7 of the key — a bright, unresolved, Steely-Dan-flavored vamp.

scales.name: Hirajoshi
scales.description: Japanese pentatonic with a dark, spacious quality. Pairs beautifully with tape-echo and reverb — a lofi jazz staple for sparse melodic hooks.

progressions.description: The two tonal centers of Hirajoshi. bVImaj7 is fully diatonic — its four notes (b6, 1, b3, 5) are exactly four of the five scale tones — so this vamp is the purest possible harmonic expression of the mode.
Same two chords, reversed emphasis. Starting on bVImaj7 lets the scale's b6 anchor the ear, creating the 'floating down onto home' resolution that's characteristic of Japanese modal music.
